title: Ashurbanipal's Library: He Was Both a Tyrant and the Earliest Book Collector
dek: Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — while building humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.
why: Medium information density; the first half is Mesopotamian background, the second half on the library's preservation and decipherment is where the value is.
who: Listeners interested in ancient civilizations, library history, archaeology and textual decipherment; anyone curious about historical judgment questions like why the same person can be both a tyrant and a patron.
skip: The opening 0:01-4:04 on Mesopotamian geography and the "cradle of civilization" setup, and the listener mail after 31:54.

points.h: The same person, two opposite first impressions
points.body: At the British Museum, Tracy read the display panels about Ashurbanipal's library and thought, "this guy's library is amazing"; in the same gallery Patrick read the other panels about him as an Assyrian king and came away thinking, "this guy was really cruel." The same material can support two completely opposite impressions, and the rest of the episode unpacks that contradiction: he did put defeated Elamite kings in his chariot and lock rivals in dog kennels, and he did order texts from across the empire copied and sent to the capital.

points.h: You can't put Mesopotamia on a timeline at all
points.body: Tracy wanted to open the episode with a basic timeline and found she couldn't. Mesopotamia spans more than three thousand years from the first cities, with civilizations, kingdoms and empires overlapping and influencing each other, so a linear timeline is itself a distortion. Assyrian history is divided into Early Assyrian (from about 2600 BCE), Old Assyrian (from about 2025 BCE), Middle Assyrian (from about 1363 BCE), Neo-Assyrian (911 to 609 BCE), followed by the post-imperial period. Assyrians still exist today: roughly three to five million people in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey identify as Assyrian.

points.h: The father split the empire in two to prevent civil war
points.body: Esarhaddon's father Sennacherib had completely destroyed Babylon and even diverted canals to flood the ruins, and was later assassinated by his own sons, which was interpreted as divine punishment for destroying Babylon. Esarhaddon rebuilt Babylon and positioned himself as its "governor" rather than king. In 672 BCE he divided responsibilities between two sons: Shamashumukin would govern Babylon, and Ashurbanipal was made crown prince of Assyria. The arrangement was meant to prevent a repeat of the civil war that had attended his own accession. The episode says explicitly that this will come back later — because the brothers eventually turned on each other.

points.h: He got an education a king wasn't supposed to have
points.body: Ashurbanipal's education had already begun when he was made crown prince. He learned horsemanship, chariot driving, archery, military tactics and court etiquette — the standard royal package. But he also studied literature and history, knew multiple Sumerian and Akkadian dialects, and could read and write cuneiform. The episode stresses that kings of this era typically did not receive such an academic education and were often illiterate; literacy was the domain of scholars and scribes. He was able to do this likely because early in life he was not fully raised as the heir to the throne.

points.h: In the reliefs, he wears a writing tool on his belt
points.body: Ashurbanipal was a patron of the arts, building temples and palaces and commissioning large numbers of reliefs. Many depict him fighting, lion hunting, and going about daily life amid wealth and luxury; some show the severed heads of enemies. The episode highlights one detail in particular: in many depictions he wears a riding stylus on his belt, including in scenes where he is killing lions with a sword — Holly jokes that he might have wanted to write a diary entry after killing a lion. The reliefs from his reign are considered the peak of Assyrian art; the lion hunt reliefs are now in the British Museum.

points.h: Cruelty wasn't his invention — he took it to the extreme
points.body: The episode draws a clear distinction: practices like displaying the severed heads of enemies were normal among rulers in ancient Mesopotamia; but in his own commissioned depictions and in records left by others, Ashurbanipal is seen as taking this to an extreme. Specific examples include: salting the land after putting down a rebellion, forcing people to grind their ancestors' bones to make bricks for a palace, making a defeated Elamite king pull his chariot in a triumphal procession, and forcing a rival to live in a dog kennel. About that rival, some accounts say he was forced to wear a dog collar, others that a chain was run through his jaw.

points.h: This was the earliest "systematic collection" library
points.body: The library was built in the capital, Nineveh, and tablets have been found in the Southwest Palace, the North Palace, and around the temples of Ishtar and Nabu. The episode stresses two points: first, it is unclear whether these were the library's original storage locations or the result of tablets scattering after the city's destruction; second, this is one of the earliest known libraries to be systematically acquired and organized, a deliberately collected and curated knowledge base, and the world's largest collection of Assyrian texts. Excavations yielded more than twenty thousand tablets and fragments, many with standardized colophons, indicating a systematic method of labeling and cataloging. The total number of complete tablets is actually unknown.

points.h: He ordered the whole empire to hand over books — and knew who to ask
points.body: Ashurbanipal ordered temples and palaces across the empire to send texts to Nineveh, usually by making a copy, with him receiving the copy or the original. Surviving documents show he actually wanted the originals, and that subordinates may have "creatively misinterpreted" the instructions in order to keep originals in their own temples or collections. Surviving correspondence also shows he knew exactly where to look for texts he wanted, and who might hold works he didn't know about but that were worth acquiring. Holly describes him as having a network of scholarly acquisition librarians. Some texts in the library were written by him, and many tablets bear colophons in his hand.

points.h: The city burned, which fired the tablets hard and preserved them
points.body: Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE, an event that both preserved and destroyed the library. As the city burned, the tablets were hardened by the heat and then protected by collapsing debris; but wooden or ivory writing boards covered in wax were largely destroyed. The tablets broke and scattered during the city's destruction, and on excavation it was often unclear where in the capital they had originally been stored. Nineteenth-century excavation worsened the scattering: Austin Henry Layard and Hormuzd Rassam began excavating Nineveh in 1849, and Rassam found another large batch of tablets in 1852; much material was sent to the British Museum, and there were also French archaeological projects, so some material is now in the Louvre.

points.h: The fragments can't be reassembled because no one recorded findspots
points.body: Many tablets bear the mark "Palace of Ashurbanipal, King of the World, King of Assyria," so it can be confirmed that tablets found at different locations belong to the same collection. But during excavation, archaeologists and workers did not fully record the specific findspot of each fragment, making it hard to tell which fragment should be joined to which. The episode says the priority at the time was getting archaeological treasures back to Britain as quickly as possible, not thoroughly recording the find context of each object. The result is that reconstruction is extremely laborious: only a small portion of tablets have been reassembled, and many remain incomplete. Since the mid-nineteenth century, an average of 35 texts have been reconstructed and transcribed each year, and a great deal of work remains.

points.h: The library itself was the key sample bank for deciphering cuneiform
points.body: Researchers first deciphered cuneiform in 1857, just a few years after the library's first tablets were discovered. One key was the Bisitun inscription: an inscription on a rock face in Iran's Zagros Mountains, today a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and like the Rosetta Stone it is in three languages — Babylonian, Old Persian and Elamite — recording the account of the Achaemenid king Darius I. Henry Rawlinson published his study of the Old Persian portion in 1849, enabling the other two languages to be translated. The library provided a large number of additional cuneiform samples and was part of the decipherment process.

points.h: Before the library was excavated, Assyrian history was almost only the enemy's account
points.body: Before this, the vast majority of information about ancient Mesopotamia and the Assyrian Empire came from the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament derived from it, as well as from Greek and Roman writers. The biblical texts focus mainly on matters relating to the Levant and Egypt, and the Greek and Roman accounts were often written centuries later; neither is a complete, detailed, layered history of the Assyrian Empire. Once the library's tablets were read, they became a source of a great deal of new historical information. The episode gives one specific example: Greek literature turned Ashurbanipal into a semi-mythical figure, Sardanapalus, blending elements of him and his brother Shamashumukin, saying he was the last king of Assyria and that he burned himself to death in his palace along with all his wealth and concubines.

terms.def: A writing system pressed into clay tablets with a reed stylus, the main medium for Assyrian and Babylonian texts.
Labeling information at the end of a tablet; library tablets often have standardized colophons, indicating a cataloging method.
911 to 609 BCE, the height of the Assyrian Empire; Ashurbanipal was one of its last kings.

Obviously, plenty of monarchs and temples and wealthy people had collections of documents and texts long before this, but this is one of the oldest known systematically acquired and organized libraries in the world. It was intentionally collected and curated as a repository of knowledge.

The sacking of Nineveh in 612 BCE both preserved and destroyed Ashurbanipal's library. As the city burned, the clay tablets hardened in the heat, and then they were protected by the fallen rubble of the city around them.
Yeah, the focus was much more on sending these archaeological treasures to England than on thoroughly documenting the context where each piece was found.
